tldr: In model predictive control (MPC) for legged robots, relaxing the approximate model's equality constraints into penalty terms turns the problem into a box-constrained QP. Combining this with contact-aware dimension reduction and a tailored interior-point solver guarantees online optimization feasibility while enabling real robot walking at a 100 Hz rate with an onboard computation time of about 4.4 ms.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DR-MPC. Control inputs are reduced via swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking. Dynamics and friction constraints are relaxed to build a box-constrained QP with a block-arrow Hessian. The tailored interior-point method (IPM) solver uses a Schur complement to perform Cholesky factorization exclusively on the reduced control input dimension, operating extremely fast.
overview:
Model predictive control (MPC) has become indispensable for agile and stable legged robot locomotion. However, running MPC on a physical robot with limited compute resources requires solving the optimization within a tight budget of a few milliseconds, all while handling state estimation and footstep trajectory generation in parallel. An even trickier issue is optimization infeasibility: unexpected terrain drops or disturbances can cause contradictions among state estimates, contact constraints, and model dynamics, leading to control failure.

The authors tackled this with an unconventional question: "Since the standard single rigid body dynamics (SRBD) model is already a coarse approximation that omits leg mass and joint compliance, why force it to be strictly satisfied as an exact equality constraint?" They propose dynamics-relaxed MPC (DR-MPC), which moves the dynamics equalities and friction cone constraints into the objective function as quadratic penalties, transforming the problem into a simple box-constrained QP (BoxQP). Because only non-empty box constraints remain, mathematically a feasible solution always exists, regardless of disturbances or timing discrepancies in contact.

Furthermore, the authors developed a contact-aware input parameterization that sets swing-leg contact forces to zero and blocks stance-leg forces across time, along with a tailored interior-point method (IPM) solver that leverages the resulting block-arrow Hessian to factor only the reduced input dimension via a Schur complement. In simulation, using the same formulation, DR-MPC achieved end-to-end median speedups of $16.0\times$ over HPIPM and $4.4\times$ over OSQP. On a physical Unitree Go1 quadruped running on a Jetson Xavier NX, it achieved full onboard 100 Hz control with a median latency of 4.48 ms, demonstrating robust traversal over diverse rough terrains including grass, gravel, and slopes.
contributions: Formulated a BoxQP MPC for legged robots that relaxes SRBD equality and friction cone constraints into penalties, mathematically guaranteeing a feasible solution without slack variables.
Integrated swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking to drastically reduce control variable dimensions while preserving short-horizon control authority.
Constructed a tailored interior-point solver leveraging the block-arrow Hessian structure to eliminate states and outputs via a Schur complement, factoring only the reduced input system.
Achieved a median solve time of 4.48 ms on the onboard computer (Jetson Xavier NX) of a physical Unitree Go1, demonstrating 100 Hz locomotion across diverse outdoor terrains.

sections.heading: Why solve an approximate model strictly? DR-MPC born from an unconventional idea
sections.summary: Legged robot MPC requires high replanning frequencies, but hard constraints cause infeasibility under disturbances. This work proposes DR-MPC, an ultra-fast control framework that removes the already-approximate single rigid body dynamics from equality constraints, relaxing them into penalties to guarantee feasibility at all times.
sections.details:
For legged robots to traverse rough terrain dynamically, model predictive control (MPC) that can instantly modify ground reaction forces in response to disturbances and contact shifts is essential. However, making MPC succeed on real hardware faces two major hurdles: computational speed and feasibility.

On a compact onboard computer, state estimation, footstep planning, and low-level torque control must run concurrently. Constructing and solving the MPC optimization problem must finish within an extremely tight real-time budget (e.g., within 10 ms). Furthermore, under conventional hard-constrained MPC, large disturbances or shifted contact timing often trigger contradictions among state estimates, dynamics, and contact constraints, making the problem infeasible and causing control to collapse.

### I-A Related Work and Challenges
To address this, researchers have explored exploiting sparsity, condensing (eliminating state variables), applying fast QP solvers like HPIPM or OSQP, and move blocking to tie inputs across prediction steps. However, while these techniques accelerate computation, they do not fundamentally resolve infeasibility when sudden contact changes cause constraints to clash. Softening state constraints by adding slack variables is another common approach, but it complicates the formulation and solver structure.

### I-B Proposed Approach
Here, the authors revisited the fact that single rigid body dynamics (SRBD), standardly used in legged robots, is already an approximation that ignores leg mass and joint compliance. The intuition was: "Since it is a coarse approximation anyway, is there really a need to strictly enforce it as an exact equality constraint?"
This paper proposes dynamics-relaxed MPC (DR-MPC), which moves residuals from the dynamics and affine friction constraints into quadratic penalties in the objective, retaining only non-empty, simple upper- and lower-bound box constraints. Structurally, this mathematically guarantees that a feasible solution always exists. Combining this with an input parameterization that eliminates swing forces and blocks inputs aligned with contact phases, plus a tailored interior-point method (IPM) solver that factors only the reduced input dimension, yields an impressive onboard median time of 4.4 ms.

### I-C Contributions
The main contributions are fourfold: (1) formulating dynamics-relaxed BoxQP for legged robot SRBD to guarantee feasibility without slack variables, (2) reducing input dimensions via swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking, (3) developing a tailored IPM solver that uses a Schur complement to factor only the reduced input system, and (4) demonstrating 100 Hz real-robot locomotion on diverse outdoor rough terrains using a Unitree Go1.

sections.heading: Standard single rigid body dynamics and limits of existing MPC
sections.summary: We review the derivation of single rigid body dynamics (SRBD) standard in convex MPC for legged robots, alongside conventional hard-constrained and soft-constrained MPC formulations. We explain the mathematical reasons why existing formulations are prone to infeasibility under disturbances.
sections.details:
### II-A Single Rigid Body Dynamics (SRBD)
This paper adopts the single rigid body model widely used in convex MPC for legged locomotion. The state vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$ consists of roll, pitch, and yaw Euler angles $\Theta$, center-of-mass position $p$, angular velocity $\omega$, and linear velocity $v$. The input vector $u \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$ stacks the ground reaction forces $f_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ for all four legs in the world frame.
Assuming small roll and pitch, fixing yaw to a reference, and neglecting gyroscopic effects yields the continuous-time linear model $\dot{x} = A_c x + B_c u + c$. This model has the convenient property that $A_c^2 = 0$. Discretizing with zero-order hold over a sampling period $\Delta t$ yields a compact stacked linear prediction equation across the entire $N$-step prediction horizon: $X = E\hat{x} + FU + G$, where $\hat{x}$ is the current estimated state.

### II-B Standard MPC Formulations (Std-Hard and Std-Soft)
Conventional hard-constrained MPC (Std-Hard) minimizes state tracking error and input norms while strictly enforcing dynamics equality constraints, foot force upper and lower limits, and 16-dimensional friction pyramid inequalities $D_k u_k$ to prevent slipping as hard constraints. However, when unexpected steps or disturbances abruptly shift the current state $\hat{x}$ or break the contact schedule, an input sequence that satisfies all constraints simultaneously may cease to exist, crashing the optimization.

On the other hand, soft-constrained MPC (Std-Soft), often used in practice, introduces non-negative slack variables $\delta_k$ on state boundary constraints with penalty weights. While this absorbs state constraint violations to preserve feasibility, physical dynamics equalities and input friction pyramid constraints remain hard, leaving challenges in solver computational burden and slack weight tuning. DR-MPC takes this a step further and fundamentally redesigns the structure.

sections.heading: Relaxing dynamics: BoxQP conversion and contact-aware input reduction
sections.summary: Moving dynamics equalities and friction pyramid constraints into quadratic penalties leaves only simple non-empty box constraints, deriving a BoxQP where a solution always exists without slack variables. Swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking dramatically compress control dimensions.
sections.details:
### III-A Dynamics-Relaxed BoxQP Formulation
DR-MPC introduces an auxiliary variable $Y$ for the friction pyramid outputs $DU$, grouping the decision variables into $\chi = \mathrm{col}(U, X, Y)$. Dynamics prediction residuals $\|X - E\hat{x} - FU - G\|^2$ and friction output residuals $\|Y - DU\|^2$ are incorporated into the objective as quadratic penalties weighted by $\rho_d$ and $\rho_f$, respectively.
The remaining constraints are solely simple upper and lower box constraints on input $U$, state $X$, and friction auxiliary variable $Y$. As long as the bounds for each variable are non-empty, their Cartesian product is also guaranteed to be non-empty. In other words, for any initial state estimate or contact schedule, optimization feasibility is 100% guaranteed structurally without slack variables.

Moreover, this formulation gives the entire Hessian a clean "block-arrow" structure. The input block $R_U$ is block-tridiagonal due to force rate-of-change penalties, while the state $X$ and friction auxiliary $Y$ blocks are purely block-diagonal and uncoupled from each other. This becomes the key to the ultra-fast solver in the next section.

### III-B Contact-Aware Input Parameterization
In receding-horizon control for legged robots, inputs closest in time require fine resolution, but coarser inputs later in the horizon do not cause instability. In addition, contact forces for airborne swing legs are nominally zero. DR-MPC leverages these physical properties to reduce the input space via a sparse mapping matrix $T$ as $U = T U_r$.
- **Swing-Force Elimination**: Force variables for legs scheduled in swing are entirely removed from the optimization.
- **Contact-Aligned Move Blocking**: Forces for stance legs are grouped across intervals. Crucially, the block boundaries are perfectly aligned with contact mode switches, preventing blocks from spanning liftoff or touchdown transitions.
Allocating fine resolution at the beginning of the horizon and coarse resolution toward the end drastically reduces the control dimension $n_r$ to be solved without sacrificing short-horizon authority. The reduced prediction matrix $F_r$ and friction matrix $D_r$ are generated directly during recursive rollout without explicitly forming the full unreduced matrices.

sections.heading: Factor only the reduced input system! A lean, tailored interior-point solver
sections.summary: Leveraging the block-arrow Hessian, states and friction outputs are eliminated via a Schur complement, allowing a Mehrotra-type interior-point solver to perform Cholesky factorization strictly on the reduced input system. Local block updates and BLASFEO ensure thorough memory and computational efficiency.
sections.details:
### IV-A Reduced Newton System and Schur Complement
After normalizing variables to $[-\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}]$, a Mehrotra predictor-corrector interior-point method (IPM) is applied. In the Newton system, the normalized decision variables split into reduced inputs $\zeta_r$ and auxiliary variables $\zeta_\xi = \mathrm{col}(\zeta_X, \zeta_Y)$.
Because of the block-arrow Hessian, the auxiliary block $H_{\xi\xi} + \Sigma_\xi$ is strictly diagonal. Inverting this block requires only element-wise reciprocals. Thus, the auxiliary step $\Delta \zeta_\xi$ can be completely eliminated algebraically (via Schur complement), condensing the system into an equation solely for the reduced control input $\Delta \zeta_r$.
Consequently, the only matrix the solver must Cholesky factorize is an $n_r \times n_r$ symmetric positive definite matrix $S$. Because Cholesky factorization costs $O(n_r^3)$, the input dimension reduction ($n_r$ compression) directly translates into a dramatic drop in computation time.

### IV-B Initialization and Warm-Starting
The previous MPC solution is retained in physical coordinates $(U, X, Y)$, shifted by the elapsed time, and projected onto the new contact mapping $T$. This warm-starting strategy maintains consistency and strict internal feasibility even across changing blocking patterns.

### IV-C Structure-Exploiting Implementation Techniques
Embedded overhead is eliminated aggressively. Zero dynamic memory allocation (heap allocation) occurs during iterations; all workspaces are pre-allocated. In addition, contributions from friction outputs to the Schur complement are computed as sums of independent local updates of at most $3 \times 3$ per leg and stage, avoiding dense, large matrix multiplications. Furthermore, dense matrix operations employ BLASFEO, a linear algebra library tailored for embedded optimization, maximizing cache efficiency and execution speed.

sections.heading: 4.4 ms on Jetson Xavier NX! Compelling validation in simulation and outdoor hardware
sections.summary: In simulation, the method achieved speedups of 16.0x over HPIPM and 4.4x over OSQP. On a physical Unitree Go1 onboard system, it completed continuous outdoor walking for over 6 minutes across grass and slopes with a median time of 4.48 ms (99.87% within 10 ms), demonstrating remarkable stability.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted using a commercial Unitree Go1 quadruped robot powered by its onboard NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX computer. State estimation, MPC formulation and solving, footstep planning, and low-level control all ran simultaneously onboard. The horizon length was $N=15$ with a nominal control rate of $100$ Hz ($10$ ms budget).

### V-B Impact of Input Parameterization (Ablation)
The effect of parameterization was validated in MuJoCo simulation. Solving all full inputs (180 variables) required a median of $46.25$ ms (locomotion score $0.367$). Introducing swing-force elimination alone cut this to $21.31$ ms ($2.2\times$ faster). Adding 5-block contact-aligned move blocking ($N_u=5$) slashed the time to $4.32$ ms—a roughly $10.7\times$ speedup—while preserving control performance (score $0.361$). Reducing blocks to 3 dropped time to $2.99$ ms, but broke contact alignment and degraded the score ($0.565$), confirming $N_u=5$ as the optimal trade-off.

### V-C Simulation Comparison of MPC Methods
Comparing end-to-end median compute time against identical formulations and standard baselines, the proposed method clocked in at **$4.44$ ms**. Under the same DR formulation, this represents a **$16.0\times$** speedup over HPIPM-DR ($71.2$ ms) and a **$4.4\times$** speedup over OSQP-DR ($19.5$ ms). It was also faster than standard Std-Hard ($5.8$ ms for HPIPM, $13.9$ ms for OSQP) and Std-Soft ($7.9$ ms for HPIPM, $17.6$ ms for OSQP), demonstrating clear computational superiority without sacrificing tracking accuracy.

### V-D Physical Robot Outdoor Locomotion Experiments
A continuous outdoor walking experiment was conducted with the Go1 (approx. $6.37$ minutes, totaling $38{,}193$ MPC updates). The course included grass and slopes with changing elevation, compliance, and friction.
The onboard end-to-end time recorded a median of **$4.48$ ms** and a 95th percentile of **$5.66$ ms**, with **$99.87\%$ of all cycles meeting the 10 ms budget**. For the relaxed friction pyramid and vertical force limits, $97.87\%$ of the optimized first-step inputs strictly satisfied the constraints, maintaining stable locomotion without severe violations. Furthermore, as shown in Fig. F1, the robot traversed diverse rough terrains—asphalt, stepping stones, gravel, and irregular stone paths—without falling.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: Fast, guaranteed-feasible MPC shaping the future of legged robots
sections.summary: By deliberately removing approximate dynamics from equality constraints and relaxing them, combined with contact-aware dimension reduction and a tailored IPM, feasible 100 Hz onboard MPC was achieved. Future work includes extending to nonlinear MPC and other robotic platforms.
sections.details:
This paper presented DR-MPC, a novel MPC framework for legged locomotion. Moving away from the conventional paradigm of forcing approximate models into rigid equality constraints, it relaxes dynamics and friction constraints into penalty terms to yield a simple box-constrained QP (BoxQP). This structurally guarantees optimization feasibility under disturbances without causing solver failure.

Furthermore, the co-design of contact-aware input parameterization (swing-force elimination + contact-aligned move blocking) and a tailored interior-point solver factoring only the reduced input dimension via a Schur complement demonstrated remarkable speedups of 16.0x over HPIPM and 4.4x over OSQP. Complete onboard execution was validated on a physical Unitree Go1 with a median time of 4.48 ms, enabling stable locomotion across varied rough terrains.

Future outlooks highlighted by the authors include extending this dynamics-relaxation philosophy to nonlinear MPC (NMPC) and deploying the approach to diverse robotic platforms beyond quadrupeds.

takeaways: When using inherently coarse approximations like the single rigid body model, relaxing them into penalties rather than enforcing strict equalities provides massive advantages in both mathematical feasibility and computational efficiency.
When blocking control variables, aligning blocks strictly with liftoff and touchdown contact mode boundaries—rather than uniform spacing—is decisive for preventing tracking performance degradation.

Rather than handing the problem to an off-the-shelf solver, co-designing a tailored solver that exploits the block-arrow Hessian to factor only the reduced subspace via Schur complement is key to achieving 100 Hz onboard control on real hardware.
limitations: Because dynamics and friction pyramids are penalty-relaxed, improper tuning of penalty weights ($\rho_d, \rho_f$) risks generating physically unachievable foot force commands (in fact, minor constraint violations of about 2.13% were observed during hardware tests).
While the Mehrotra-type interior-point solver is practically very fast, a certified worst-case execution time is not mathematically guaranteed (a maximum overrun spike of 33.71 ms was observed).

Because the method is a linear time-varying MPC based on single rigid body dynamics (SRBD), applying it to tasks where full-body kinematics and nonlinearities dominate—such as climbing extreme ledges or acrobatic maneuvers—requires further extensions.
